heroIntro: In Bangladesh's vibrant commercial ecosystem, millions of taka change hands daily on the strength of a handshake, personal trust, or verbal promises between business associates, friends, or relatives. Goods are delivered, contractor services rendered, or personal loans extended without executing a formal stamp agreement. When the debtor suddenly defaults, cuts off communication, and brazenly challenges the creditor by saying, 'Show me where I signed,' creditors assume all hope is lost. Fortunately, under the Contract Act 1872, the Evidence Act 1872, and the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, oral contracts are fully valid and enforceable in Bangladesh. Here is the comprehensive legal roadmap to successfully proving an oral agreement, recovering your debt through a Money Suit, and securing court decrees.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: Can You Legally Recover Money Based on an Oral Agreement in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Yes. Under Section 10 of the Contract Act 1872, an agreement does not require a written deed to be legally valid unless specifically mandated by statute (such as land sales). Under Sections 59 and 60 of the Evidence Act 1872, all facts except the contents of documents may be proved by direct oral evidence. If you loaned money or supplied goods on a verbal agreement, you can file a formal Money Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge. To succeed, you must corroborate the verbal contract using bank transfer slips, mobile financial statements (bKash/Nagad), WhatsApp messages, email acknowledgments, and credible witness testimonies, while filing within the strict 3-year statutory deadline under Article 115 of the Limitation Act 1908.
highlights: Oral contracts are legally enforceable under Section 10 of the Contract Act 1872.
The Evidence Act 1872 permits proof of verbal debt through direct oral and electronic corroboration.
The statutory limitation period to file a Money Suit for breach of contract is exactly 3 years under the Limitation Act 1908.
Courts can grant pre-judgment attachment of the debtor's bank accounts and assets under Order 38 CPC.
points: Step 1: Compile all secondary documentary and digital proof (bank deposits, WhatsApp chats, delivery receipts).
Step 2: Dispatch a formal Advocate Legal Notice demanding payment within 15–30 days under postal registered acknowledgment.
Step 3: If no settlement occurs, institute a Money Suit in the Joint District Judge Court within the 3-year limitation window.
Step 4: File an urgent interlocutory petition under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC for Attachment Before Judgment to secure the debtor's assets.

sections.title: The Reality of Unwritten Commercial Agreements in Bangladesh
sections.content:
Across the wholesale hubs of Khatunganj in Chattogram, Chawkbazar and Islampur in Old Dhaka, and suburban industrial zones, traditional commerce still relies heavily on verbal trust. Suppliers ship consignments of raw materials worth tens of lakhs of taka on oral phone orders; contractors begin construction based on informal promises; and friends or relatives advance substantial sums during family emergencies without requesting formal promissory notes.

However, when personal relationships sour, business ventures fail, or debtors turn dishonest, the lack of a stamped written agreement becomes an acute crisis. The defaulting party often counts on the common myth that 'without a signature on non-judicial stamp paper, no case can stand in court.' Creditors frequently feel paralyzed by this misconception, delaying legal consultation until statutory limitation periods expire. Knowing how statutory civil law treats unwritten promises transforms what seems like a hopeless situation into an actionable, winnable judicial recovery.

sections.title: Contract Act 1872: The Statutory Validity of Oral Contracts
sections.content:
The foundational statute governing all contractual relationships in Bangladesh is the Contract Act 1872. Section 10 of the Act sets out what agreements are contracts: 'All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.'

Crucially, Section 10 does not state that a contract must be written. It specifically adds: 'Nothing herein contained shall affect any law in force in Bangladesh, by which any contract is required to be made in writing or in the presence of witnesses, or any law relating to the registration of documents.' While specific laws explicitly mandate written, registered deeds for transactions like land transfers (Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908) or trusts, commercial debts, loans, supply agreements, and service contracts do not require written deeds. Under settled principles upheld by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, an oral contract containing a clear offer, unequivocal acceptance, and lawful consideration is 100% legally binding and enforceable.

Creditors holding signed loan acknowledgments or IOUs printed on plain white paper instead of non-judicial stamp paper should review unstamped agreement admissibility and Section 35 tenfold penalty rules before marking exhibits at trial.

sections.title: Evidence Act 1872: Proving Verbal Agreements in Court
sections.content:
While establishing an oral agreement is legally permissible, the primary battleground in court is evidentiary proof. Under Section 59 of the Evidence Act 1872, all facts, except the contents of documents, may be proved by oral evidence. However, Section 60 mandates that oral evidence must in all cases whatever be direct—meaning that if it refers to a fact which could be heard, it must be the evidence of a witness who says he heard it.

When an oral debt is contested, the plaintiff cannot rely solely on their own uncorroborated oral statement. The court demands a coherent narrative supported by credible third-party witnesses who were physically present when the money was handed over, when the terms were negotiated, or when the debtor subsequently acknowledged the debt and promised repayment. Depositions from business partners, shop managers, or shared associates who witnessed the transaction form the oral foundation of your plaint.

sections.title: Crucial Evidence: Bank Statements, SMS, and Chat Logs
sections.content:
In modern commercial litigation, contemporaneous electronic and financial records provide the definitive corroboration that elevates an oral contract into an unassailable court claim. Key evidentiary categories include:

  • Banking Audit Trails: Cheque counterfoils, bank account debit advice, RTGS/BEFTN transfer slips, and deposit receipts showing funds moving directly from your account to the debtor's account. This disproves any claim that no money ever changed hands.
  • Mobile Financial Services (MFS): Verified transaction statements from bKash, Nagad, or Rocket detailing transaction IDs, sender/receiver wallet numbers, and timestamps.
  • Electronic Messages & WhatsApp Chats: WhatsApp conversations, SMS messages, and emails where the debtor discusses the transaction, acknowledges the debt, requests more time to pay, or apologizes for default. Under Section 65B of the Evidence Act, printouts of electronic records accompanied by certificate of authenticity are admissible.
  • Chalan and Delivery Slips: Signed goods delivery challans, gate passes, store ledger entries, or transport receipts proving physical handover of merchandise.

When these paper and digital trails corroborate witness testimony, civil judges readily find in favor of the plaintiff.

sections.title: Mandatory Limitation Deadlines: Article 115 Limitation Act
sections.content:
The single most dangerous trap for creditors seeking to recover an oral debt is the law of limitation. Under the Limitation Act 1908, the state will not aid a creditor who sleeps on their legal rights. Unlike debts backed by registered mortgage deeds (which enjoy longer limitation windows), oral contracts are subject to strict, abbreviated deadlines.

Under Article 115 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act 1908, for compensation for the breach of any contract, express or implied, not in writing registered and not specifically provided for, the limitation period is exactly three (3) years. The three-year countdown begins from the date when the contract is broken—meaning the date on which the debtor failed to repay the money as promised, or the date of the last partial payment or written acknowledgment of liability under Section 19 of the Limitation Act. If you file your Money Suit three years and one day after the cause of action arose, the civil court is statutorily mandated to dismiss your suit under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, regardless of how genuine your claim is.

sections.title: Drafting and Serving the Advocate Legal Notice
sections.content:
Before approaching the civil court to institute a formal Money Suit, serving a formal Advocate Legal Notice is a mandatory strategic prerequisite. The legal notice achieves several decisive objectives:

  1. Establishes Formal Demand: It places on record the exact dates, amounts, bank transaction references, and verbal terms agreed upon, demanding full settlement within a specified deadline (usually 15 to 30 days).
  2. Fixes the Cause of Action: It formally establishes the date of default, crystallizing the cause of action for the subsequent Money Suit.
  3. Opportunity for Acknowledgment: If the debtor replies to the legal notice through their advocate, even a partial admission or evasive reply serves as written evidence that an underlying transaction existed, destroying their defense that they never knew you.

The legal notice must be dispatched via Registered Post with Acknowledgment Due (AD) to the debtor's residential and business addresses, and postal receipts and signed AD cards must be preserved as primary suit exhibits.

sections.title: Money Suit Procedure in the Joint District Judge Court
sections.content:
If the legal notice period expires without payment, your advocate files a Money Suit under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. In Bangladesh, pecuniary jurisdiction determines the forum: suits involving substantial commercial sums (typically exceeding BDT 25,00,000) are instituted in the Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction where the debtor resides or where the cause of action arose.

The litigation progresses through defined stages: filing of the plaint with ad-valorem court fees; service of summons on the defendant; filing of the Written Statement (WS) by the debtor; framing of issues by the court; alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mediation under Section 89A CPC; and the trial stage where the plaintiff and supporting witnesses take the stand for examination-in-chief and cross-examination. Upon reviewing the oral testimonies and electronic exhibits, the court delivers a Money Decree specifying the principal sum plus statutory interest from the date of default.

sections.title: Order 38 CPC: Attachment of Debtor Assets Before Judgment
sections.content:
A major concern in commercial debt recovery is that while the Money Suit is pending, the debtor will sell off their properties, withdraw bank balances, or transfer assets to relatives, rendering an ultimate decree a hollow victory. To prevent this, the law provides an aggressive interlocutory remedy under Order 38, Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC): Attachment Before Judgment.

Under Order 38 Rule 5, where the court is satisfied that the defendant, with intent to obstruct or delay the execution of any decree that may be passed against him, is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property or remove it from local jurisdiction, the court may direct the defendant to furnish security, and failing that, order the interim attachment of their immovable properties, commercial inventories, or bank accounts. Securing an Order 38 attachment freezes the debtor's financial mobility, often compelling them to negotiate an immediate out-of-court settlement.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Recovering BDT 18 Lakh on an Oral Deal
sections.content:
The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) demonstrates how a structured Money Suit recovered substantial funds without a written deed in Dhaka:

A garment accessories manufacturer in Tongi supplied zipper and button consignments valued at BDT 18,50,000 to a buying house in Uttara based entirely on verbal telephone orders and WhatsApp requests. The supplier delivered the goods across four consignments with signed delivery receipts. However, the buyer delayed payment for eight months, offering verbal excuses. Eventually, the buyer blocked the supplier's calls and informed third parties that because there was no stamped contract, the supplier could never recover the money.

The manufacturer retained an experienced civil litigation advocate. Within one week, the advocate served a comprehensive Legal Notice via registered post, detailing the four delivery dates, attaching the signed delivery challans, and quoting verbatim WhatsApp messages where the buyer acknowledged receipt and promised payment by 'next month.' When the buyer ignored the notice, the advocate filed a Money Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, within the three-year limitation period. Simultaneously, they moved an application under Order 38 Rule 5 CPC for interim attachment of the buyer's corporate bank account, proving that the buyer was preparing to close the firm.

Faced with a frozen bank account and confronted with unassailable electronic and delivery records, the debtor's counsel approached the court during pre-trial mediation under Section 89A CPC. The parties executed a court-sanctioned Solenama (compromise decree): the debtor paid BDT 10,00,000 upfront via bank pay order and the remaining BDT 8,50,000 in two post-dated cheques backed by personal guarantees, achieving 100% debt recovery without enduring a full multi-year trial.

faqs.question: Is an oral contract legally binding in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 10 of the Contract Act 1872, an agreement does not need to be in writing to be legally enforceable, provided it contains mutual consent, competent parties, lawful consideration, and a lawful object. Oral contracts are valid unless a specific statute explicitly mandates written registration.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a lawsuit for an unpaid oral debt?
faqs.answer: Under Article 115 of the Limitation Act 1908, the statutory limitation period to file a Money Suit for breach of an unwritten contract is strictly three (3) years from the date of default or from the date of the last partial repayment or written acknowledgment.

faqs.question: Can I use WhatsApp messages and SMS to prove an oral agreement in court?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under modern evidentiary practice and Section 65B of the Evidence Act, digital communications such as WhatsApp chats, text messages, and emails acknowledging the debt or discussing delivery terms are fully admissible as electronic corroboration.

faqs.question: What court do I file a Money Suit in for recovering business debts?
faqs.answer: Money Suits are filed in the Civil Court based on pecuniary jurisdiction. Modest claims are heard by Senior Assistant Judges, while substantial commercial claims (typically above BDT 25,00,000) are filed in the Court of the Joint District Judge.

faqs.question: What is an Order 38 Rule 5 CPC attachment before judgment?
faqs.answer: It is an emergency civil court order that temporarily freezes the debtor's bank accounts, real estate, or commercial inventories while the lawsuit is ongoing, preventing them from hiding or selling assets before the decree is passed.

faqs.question: Do I have to pay court fees to file a Money Suit in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Money Suits require an ad-valorem court fee calculated as a percentage of the claimed debt amount under the Court-fees Act 1870, subject to a statutory maximum cap. If you win the suit, the court typically decrees that the debtor must reimburse your court fees and legal costs.

faqs.question: Can an oral debt be converted into a criminal case under Section 420 Penal Code?
faqs.answer: If the debtor had fraudulent intentions from the very inception (such as providing fake identities or non-existent company names), a criminal case for cheating under Section 420 and criminal breach of trust under Section 406 can be filed alongside or prior to civil recovery.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) sue for unpaid business money from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. An NRB creditor can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the local Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, appointing a representative or advocate in Bangladesh to institute and prosecute the Money Suit on their behalf.
